Leishmaniasis

One uncontrolled pilot reported 91% complete and 9% partial response in Grade I-II cutaneous disease and no response in Grade III-V; subgroup denominators were not stated in the abstract.

Clinical effect sizes (estimate)

Grade I-II cutaneous disease — At 10 months, the pilot reported 91% complete and 9% partial response. It reported no response in Grade III-V disease. The abstract does not state subgroup denominators or confidence intervals. There was no control arm, so these percentages are descriptive rather than comparative (Khan et al. 2020).

Certainty of evidence (estimate)

Very low certainty for early-stage cutaneous lesion response. The single-arm pilot treated 53 people and reported 123 clustered lesions; it gives no subgroup denominators or confidence intervals. A controlled study with patient-level allocation and standardized disease grades is needed (Khan et al. 2020).

PBM Database summary

What the records report

One uncontrolled pilot reported 91% complete and 9% partial response in Grade I-II cutaneous disease and no response in Grade III-V; subgroup denominators were not stated in the abstract.

Summary of the Evidence

One human single-arm pilot studied 53 people with cutaneous leishmaniasis and 123 lesions. Lesions were nested within patients, so 123 is not the number of independent participants. The report separated early-grade lesions from advanced disease. No randomized or controlled PBM study, animal experiment, or separate in-vitro study for cutaneous leishmaniasis was identified in the relevant database category.

Human and clinical evidence

The pilot used laser treatment four times over four weeks and followed participants for ten months. At follow-up, complete response was reported in 91% and partial response in 9% of patients with Grade I-II disease; no response was reported for Grade III-V disease. The abstract does not state subgroup denominators or confidence intervals. Because there was no control arm and the 123 lesions were clustered within 53 people, these percentages do not establish a causal PBM effect (Khan et al. 2020).

Animal evidence

No animal study directly evaluating PBM for cutaneous leishmaniasis was identified.

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

No separate parasite, cell-culture, or tissue experiment directly testing PBM for this indication was identified in the mapped evidence.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The investigators applied a 635-nm red visible laser at 300 mW and 75 J/cm² to the lesions, with four weekly sessions. The study did not compare wavelengths, fluences, or schedules. These parameters therefore describe one pilot protocol and do not establish an optimal dose. The marked difference between early- and advanced-grade results also limits generalization across lesion severity.

Interpretation

The pilot reported responses for Grade I-II disease and no response for Grade III-V disease at ten months. Without subgroup denominators, confidence intervals, or a control group, this is a descriptive pattern within one small sample, not a comparative treatment estimate. A controlled trial should use patient-level allocation, standardize lesion grading, and report parasitological outcomes alongside usual care.

Rationale for the certainty assessment

One uncontrolled pilot reported 91% complete and 9% partial response in early-grade disease, but the abstract does not state subgroup denominators or confidence intervals. All 53 participants received PBM, and the 123 lesions were clustered within those people. A controlled trial with patient-level allocation and standardized lesion grading is needed (Khan et al. 2020).
